extracted.intended_audience: jurors, judges, and attorneys in U.S. federal patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions covering patent conception/reduction to practice, novelty/anticipation, prior art, obviousness (including level of ordinary skill and secondary considerations), inventorship, equitable defenses (inequitable conduct, laches, equitable estoppel, prosecution laches, unclean hands), and patent damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is the mental part of an inventive act: the formation in the mind of the inventor of a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention as it is thereafter to be applied in practice, even if the inventor did not know at the time that the invention would work. Conception of an invention is complete when the idea is so clearly defined in the inventor’s mind that, if the idea were communicated to a person having ordinary skill in the field of the technology, he or she would be able to reduce the invention to practice without undue research or experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not require a prototype or that the inventor actually explained the invention to another person. There must be some evidence beyond the inventor’s own testimony that confirms the date of conception. Conception may be proven when the invention is shown in its complete form by drawings, disclosure to another person, or other forms of evidence presented at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (in reduction to practice context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence means working continuously, though not necessarily every day, in the period between conception and reducing the invention to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess whether an inventor exercised continuous efforts to reduce the conceived invention to practice; relevant in priority disputes/interference contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is 'reduced to practice' when it has been constructed/used/tested sufficiently to show that it will work for its intended purpose or when the inventor files a patent application. An invention may also be reduced to practice even if the inventor has not made or tested a prototype if it has been fully described in a filed patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice can be actual (constructing/using/testing) or constructive (filing a sufficiently detailed patent application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (pre-March 16, 2013 novelty standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents having an effective filing date before March 16, 2013: to be entitled to a patent, the invention must be 'new' and inventor must not have lost rights by delaying filing. Anticipation must be determined claim-by-claim. [Alleged infringer] must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claim(s) is/are invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a list of ways a claim can be shown not new or the patentee lost rights (choose applicable): (1) known to or used by others in the U.S. before [date of invention] (publicly accessible); (2) already patented or described in a printed publication anywhere in the world before [date of invention]; (3) patented or described in a printed publication by patentee or anyone else more than a year before the effective filing date (on-sale/publication bars); (4) publicly used, sold, or offered for sale in the U.S. more than one year before effective filing date; (5) abandonment of the invention; (6) foreign patenting or foreign filing more than one year before U.S. filing; (7) described in a published patent application by another in the U.S. (or PCT designated and published in English) before [date of invention]; (8) described in a patent granted on an application by another filed before [relevant date]; (9) not invented by the named inventor; (10) made by someone else in the U.S. before patentee and not abandoned/suppressed/concealed. If an interference proceeding exists, additional instructions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art (post-March 16, 2013 / AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents having an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, prior art may include: (1) items publicly known or used, on sale, or otherwise made available to the public before the filing date; (2) publications made available to the public before the filing date; (3) patents and published patent applications naming another inventor that were filed before the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: prior art does not include an item/publication that is the inventor’s own work, describes the inventor’s own work, or was obtained from the inventor (unless made public more than one year before filing). Also excludes patents/applications that disclose the inventor’s own work or were obtained from/owned by the same person (with similar one-year exception). For anticipation analysis, the alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that all claim requirements were present in a single prior reference (expressly or implicitly) so a person of ordinary skill could make and use the claimed invention from that one reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must not have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the time the invention was made or before the filing date to be patentable. [Alleged infringer] may establish invalidity by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider level of ordinary skill, scope and content of the prior art, and differences between prior art and claimed invention. Existence of each element of claim in prior art does not necessarily prove obviousness—many inventions build on prior art. Factors to consider whether a person would have been prompted to combine known elements include: (1) predictable result of using prior art elements per known functions; (2) obvious solution to a known problem; (3) prior art teaches/suggests combining elements; (4) prior art teaches away from combining elements; (5) 'obvious to try' when finite predictable solutions exist and design/market pressure exists (but 'obvious to try' not sufficient in unpredictable technologies); (6) whether change resulted more from design incentives or market forces. To find obviousness, prior art must provide a reasonable expectation of success. Do not use hindsight; evaluate claim-by-claim. Consider objective (secondary) evidence such as commercial success, long-felt need, failed attempts by others, contemporaneous invention by others, copying, unexpected results, praise, expressions of surprise, licensing, and departure from accepted wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective Evidence / Secondary Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that may shed light on obviousness (sometimes called secondary considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of factors to consider: (a) commercial success due to merits of claimed invention (not marketing); (b) satisfied a long-felt need; (c) others tried and failed; (d) others invented at roughly same time; (e) others copied invention; (f) contemporaneous changes in related tech or market needs; (g) invention achieved unexpected results; (h) praise from others in the field; (i) expressions of surprise or disbelief by persons of ordinary skill; (j) others sought/obtained rights from patent holder; (k) inventor proceeded contrary to accepted wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of Ordinary Skill in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding the level of ordinary skill in the field of the invention, consider all evidence introduced at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include but are not limited to: (1) levels of education and experience of the inventor and others working in the field; (2) types of problems encountered in the field; (3) prior art solutions to those problems; (4) rapidity with which innovations are made; (5) sophistication of the technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Content of the Prior Art (for obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the scope and content of the prior art when assessing obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope includes prior art in the same field and prior art from different fields that a person of ordinary skill might combine using common sense. If attacking party relies on prior art considered by the Examiner during prosecution, that party bears the burden of overcoming deference to the agency. In combination-based invalidity defenses, use a flexible analysis considering whether the prior art teaches, suggests, or motivates the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is invalid if it fails to name all and only the actual inventors. To be an inventor, one must make a significant contribution to the conception of at least one or more of the claims of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance of contribution is measured against the scope of the full invention. Merely explaining well-known concepts or the state of the art, or merely carrying out experiments under instructions, does not make someone an inventor. Persons may be co-inventors even if they contributed different types/amounts or did not contribute to each claim, but they must have had some open line of communication during or near the inventive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequitable conduct occurs when a person involved in prosecution fails to supply material information or supplies false information or statements to the PTO with intent to deceive, rendering any patent issued unenforceable as a matter of fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden: alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence both (1) that a person meaningfully involved in prosecution withheld material information or submitted materially false information/statements, and (2) that the person did so with intent to deceive the Examiner. Material: information is material if PTO would not have allowed the claim had it been aware; false/misleading statement is material if it convinces PTO to allow a claim it would not have. Affirmative egregious misconduct (e.g., filing an unmistakably false affidavit) may be material. Intent to deceive: negligence, oversight, carelessness, or even gross negligence does not establish intent. Intent can be direct (documents/testimony) or inferred, but may be inferred only where it is the single most reasonable inference from the evidence. Materiality and intent are separate; both must be proven by clear and convincing evidence to find inequitable conduct and unenforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense that patent holder delayed filing suit unreasonably and that the alleged infringer was prejudiced as a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged infringer must prove (by preponderance) (1) unreasonably long and inexcusable delay by patent holder, and (2) material prejudice to alleged infringer. No minimum delay required; a six-year delay gives rise to a rebuttable presumption that delay was unreasonable and prejudicial (shifts burden to patent holder to justify delay). Justifying facts for delay include involvement in other litigation, negotiations, poverty/illness, wartime conditions, disputes about ownership, or minimal infringing activity. Prejudice can be evidentiary (lost records, witness death, faded memories) or economic (changed economic position beyond merely paying for infringement, e.g., inability to switch to noninfringing product). Even if elements are proved, laches may not apply if fairness dictates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holder may be estopped from relief where: (1) the patent holder communicated misleadingly to the infringer about lack of infringement or lack of litigation; (2) the infringer relied on that misleading communication; (3) the infringer will be materially harmed if patent holder is allowed to assert a claim inconsistent with its prior misleading communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged infringer must prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence, but equitable estoppel need not be found even if elements are proven if finding it would be unfair. Communication can be written, spoken, conduct, silence, or a combination. Harm can be evidentiary (inability to present a full defense due to lost records/witnesses) or economic (changed economic position such that losses could have been avoided). Consider facts and circumstances as they existed at the time of the communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution Laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense that owner is barred from enforcing claims due to unreasonably long delay in filing the claims of the patent and resulting prejudice to infringer, another private party, or the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay measured from the original application filing to the filing of the asserted patent. Determine whether delay was unreasonably long by considering facts/circumstances during the delay. Consider whether others invested in developing/manufacturing/selling products covered by the asserted patent during the delay, whether public practice of the invention was unfairly postponed, whether delay was intentional, and whether infringer/public were aware of pending applications. Authorities note prosecution laches may bar enforcement even if statutes/rules were followed when delay was unreasonable and unexplained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclean Hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Owner may be barred from enforcing a patent where the owner acted inequitably, unfairly, or deceitfully toward the infringer or the Court in a way that has immediate and necessary relation to the relief sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged infringer must prove unclean hands by a preponderance of the evidence. Jury should weigh all facts and circumstances to determine whether, on balance, the patent holder acted so unfairly in matters relating to the controversy that, in fairness, relief should be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—Measure and Burden
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement of any valid claim is found, damages must adequately compensate the patent holder for the infringement and are not punitive. Patent holder has burden to establish amount of damages by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages should put patent holder in approximately the same financial position as if infringement had not occurred. Types of damages include lost profits (actual reduction in business profits due to infringement) and reasonable royalty (amount the parties would have agreed upon as a fee for the use of the invention at a time before infringement began). Patent holder is entitled to recover no less than a reasonable royalty for each infringing act. More detailed instructions may be provided for specific damage theories (e.g., price erosion, convoyed sales) as appropriate.
